newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Child's play and mob justice in new Congo capital.
newsitem.headline: Child's play and mob justice in new Congo capital.

text.p: In the looted wreckage of ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko's Kinshasa home, excited children scavenge books.
It's the latest game on their block -- and books are worth money, aren't they?
In another room, an angry man takes a blunt instrument to a painting of the veteran strongman's face.
Across Kinshasa, slowly regaining a semblance of normality after Laurent Kabila's rebels marched in at the weekend, the pattern is the same.
A mix of innocent celebration and more sinister score-settling.
In the main market place, a suspected member Mobutu's once-feared presidential guard is beaten to death.
Others are luckier -- a little.
In the town centre, a mob tries to "necklace" another suspected presidential guard. In the confusion, he shakes off the tyres and survives.
In another corner of town, a mob strips and beats a woman accused of working for the man who dominated Africa's third largest nation for three decades. Passing rebels intervene.
Elsewhere, groups of sullen young men face an uncertain fate.
In Camp Mobutu, renamed Camp Kabila, rebel soldiers bring in one group of up to 20 Rwandan males in their 20s -- from Kinshasa's main Mama Yemo hospital.
They include amputees, though none has fresh wounds. They are suspected members of Rwanda's former Hutu army, which fought alongside Mobutu's soldiers.
In one incident, young rebels club suspects with rifle butts and threaten them with execution. Older brothers in arms intervene and restrain them -- for the time being.
But for many in the city, impoverished by three decades of Mubutu rule, things can only get better.
Critics accuse Mobutu and his clan of plundering one of Africa's richest nations while leaving its people to struggle with poverty.
Up to 2,000 students and workers took to the streets on Monday, waving tree branches in an impromptu tribute to the man who rid them of Mobutu.
Kabila, the self-proclaimed president of the renamed Democratic Republic of Congo, is due in town on Tuesday,
In the meantime, his troops have been scouring the city for weapons, which they collect and stack in military camps.
But businessmen, keen to get back to normal, say security remains a major problem.
Armed men in uniform, believed to be from Mobutu's routed army and security agencies, stage hold-ups and loot.
Rebel spokesmen say they will soon have up to 20,000 fighters in town to stamp that out.
